# Volume 5 — CHAPTER III. THE HOLLOWMERE CHILDREN

!!! note "Source text"
    Passages cited on the wiki pages link into this page. Only volumes at or before
    this page's cutoff are present.

During the day, playing amid the lush, quiet verdure and shadows of the large maple grove situated between Hollowmere and the Glen St. Agnes pond suited the Carrow children very much; however, when it came to night-time fun, no spot surpassed the small valley lying behind the maple grove. To them, it served as an enchanted kingdom of wonder. On one occasion, while gazing out of the attic windows at Hollowmere through the haze and wake of a summer thunderstorm, they had observed a magnificent rainbow spanning over their cherished location, with one of its ends appearing to plunge directly into the place where a bend of the pond extended into the valley's bottom end.
{: #nw-v05-c03-p0000 }

“We should name it Fern Hollow,” Edmund remarked with joy, and from that moment onward, Fern Hollow became its name.
{: #nw-v05-c03-p0001 }

Beyond Fern Hollow, the gales could be boisterous and rollicking. In this spot, the breeze invariably moved with gentleness. Small, twisting, enchanted tracks coursed to and fro across spruce roots that moss cushioned. Scattered throughout the valley, blending with the dark spruces, were wild cherry trees that would turn misty white when in bloom. Originating from the Glen village, a tiny stream filled with amber waters flowed through the area. The homes of the village stood at a comfortably distant range; just at the top part of the valley was a small, dilapidated, abandoned cottage, known as “the old Bailey house.” No one had lived in it for numerous years, yet an embankment covered in grass encircled it, and contained within was an ancient garden in which the Hollowmere children were able to discover violets, daisies, and June lilies still flowering when the time came. As for the remainder, the garden was smothered in caraway that, during the moonshine of summer evenings, billowed and surged like silver seas.
{: #nw-v05-c03-p0002 }

To the south, the pond was situated, and past it, the ripe landscape faded into purple forests, except where an isolated, ancient gray farmhouse situated on a lofty hill overlooked both the glen and the harbour. A particular untamed woodland quality and seclusion characterized Fern Hollow, regardless of how close it was to the village, making the children of Hollowmere fond of it.
{: #nw-v05-c03-p0003 }

Dear, friendly hollows filled the valley, and their most cherished spot was the biggest one among them. On this specific night, they had gathered in this place. A grove of young spruces stood within this hollow, surrounding a small, grassy glade at its center that opened onto the stream's bank. Alongside the stream grew a silver birch-tree, a young and remarkably straight growth that Edmund had dubbed the “White Lady.” Within this glade as well stood the “Tree Lovers,” the name Edmund gave to a spruce and maple growing in such close proximity that their branches were inextricably tangled together. Kit had suspended an old strand of sleigh-bells, which he received from the Glen blacksmith, upon the Tree Lovers, and each passing breeze elicited unexpected, magical tinkling sounds from it.
{: #nw-v05-c03-p0004 }

“It is so wonderful returning here!” Bess remarked. “When all is said and done, not a single one of the Brierley locations can truly compare to Fern Hollow.”
{: #nw-v05-c03-p0005 }

Even so, they held the Brierley locations in high regard. Going to Grey Shutters was constantly viewed as a wonderful delight. Aunt Thirza treated them very kindly, as did Mrs. Agatha Sowerby, who occupied her remaining years in crafting cotton-warp quilts for when Nell’s daughters required a “setting-out.” Furthermore, delightful companions were present there—“Uncle” Robin’s children along with “Aunt” Isolde’s children. They were acquainted with every location their mother had treasured so deeply during her youth at former Grey Shutters—the lengthy Linger Lane, which possessed pink hedges when wild roses bloomed, the perpetually tidy yard, featuring its willows and poplars, the Nymph’s Well, clear and beautiful just like in the past, the Lake of Glassy Waters, and Reedmere. The twins occupied their mother’s former porch-gable room, and Aunt Thirza was accustomed to entering after dark, whenever she believed they had fallen asleep, to gaze at them fondly. Nevertheless, everyone was aware that she cherished Kit most of all.
{: #nw-v05-c03-p0006 }

Kit was currently very busy frying a batch of little trout that he had recently taken from the pond. A ring of red stones surrounding a burning fire formed his stove, while his cooking gear comprised a flattened old tin can and a fork that retained just a single tine. Even so, splendid dishes had previously been cooked in this manner.
{: #nw-v05-c03-p0007 }

Kit was the offspring who belonged to the House of Dreams. Every other child had come into the world at Hollowmere. His red hair curled just like his mother’s, while his open hazel eyes resembled his father’s; his fine nose was inherited from his mother, and his father gave him a steady, humorous mouth. Furthermore, he was the sole member of the family whose ears were pleasant enough to satisfy Tabitha. Nevertheless, a continuous quarrel existed between him and Tabitha, owing to her refusal to stop addressing him as Little Kit. Thirteen-year-old Kit considered this intolerable. Mother possessed better judgment.
{: #nw-v05-c03-p0008 }

“On the day he turned eight, he had exclaimed with indignation, “Mother, I’m not little any more. I’m awful big.””
{: #nw-v05-c03-p0009 }

With a sigh, a laugh, and another sigh, Mother ceased to address him as Little Kit ever again—or at least, never within his earshot.
{: #nw-v05-c03-p0010 }

He had always been, as he was still, a dependable and solid little fellow. Promises were something he never broke. Speech did not come from him in great amounts. Though his teachers failed to see brilliance in him, his scholastic abilities were solid and well-rounded. Taking matters on trust was not his way; instead, he preferred to personally test the accuracy of any assertion. On one occasion, Tabitha had warned him that contacting a frost-covered latch with his tongue would cause all its skin to be ripped away. Immediately, Kit had proceeded to do so, “just to see if it was so.” The result proved to him that it was “so,” leaving him to endure a painful tongue for a number of days. Even so, Kit did not mind the pain when it served the cause of science. Through continual observation and testing, he acquired much information, and his vast acquaintance with their small environment struck his brothers and sisters as truly remarkable. Kit was always aware of the locations of the earliest and most mature berries, the places where the initial light-colored violets timidly awoke from their cold season of rest, and the exact count of blue eggs inside any specified robin’s nest within the maple grove. Reading fortunes using daisy petals, extracting honey from red clovers, and digging out various kinds of eatable roots along the pond's edge were all things he could do, whereas Tabitha lived in constant dread that the entire group would end up poisoned. He possessed knowledge of the locations containing the most superior spruce-gum, which appeared as light amber lumps upon the lichen-covered bark, he was aware of the spots where nuts clustered most densely within the beechwoods surrounding the Harbour Head, and he knew the finest locations for trout fishing higher up the streams. Any call made by a wild bird or animal in Seven Gulls could be imitated by him, and from spring until autumn, he was familiar with the home of every wild flower.
{: #nw-v05-c03-p0011 }

Beside Edmund Carrow lay a book of poetry as he sat beneath the White Lady, yet reading was not what occupied him. His large, magnificent eyes were filled with delight as he looked first at the willows shrouded in emerald mist beside the pond, and then toward Fern Hollow, where a drift of clouds, resembling small silver sheep driven by the breeze, passed overhead. Extraordinary indeed were the eyes of Edmund. From within their deep gray recesses, the collective happiness, grief, mirth, devotion, and longing of numerous buried ancestors seemed to gaze forth.
{: #nw-v05-c03-p0012 }

In terms of appearance, Edmund was a “hop out of kin.” No recognized family member looked like him. Featuring well-shaped features and straight black hair, he was easily the most handsome among the children of Hollowmere. Yet he possessed the exact same intense love of beauty and lively imagination as his mother. Winter’s frost, spring’s invitation, summer’s dream, and autumn’s glamour every one held great meaning for Edmund.
{: #nw-v05-c03-p0013 }

At school, an institution where Kit held the status of a chieftain, Edmund enjoyed little esteem. Because he never engaged in fights and rarely participated in the school's sports, choosing instead to isolate himself in secluded spots to read books—most notably “po’try books”—he was considered to be “girly” and milk-soppish. Edmund adored the poets and spent hours engrossed in their writings from the moment he learned to read. Their melody—the melody of the immortals—interwove itself into his developing soul. It was Edmund's cherished desire to become a poet himself one day. Such an achievement was possible. Edmund took as his pattern a certain Uncle Cedric—a title granted out of courtesy—who currently resided in that enigma of a place known as “the States.” Uncle Cedric had formerly been a young student in Brierley, and at present, people everywhere read his poetry. Nevertheless, the Glen schoolboys remained unaware of Edmund’s ambitions, nor would they have been much awed had they known. Even with his deficiency in physical strength, he nevertheless extracted a degree of reluctant admiration through his ability for “talking book talk.” No pupil in Glen St. Agnes school possessed his manner of speech. He “sounded like a preacher,” a boy remarked; consequently, he was usually left in peace rather than being targeted, unlike the majority of boys who were thought to abhor or dread fighting.
{: #nw-v05-c03-p0014 }

The Hollowmere twins, who were ten years old, broke twin tradition because they did not look the slightest bit similar. Nell, whom everyone called Bess, possessed great beauty, featuring silky nut-brown hair alongside velvety nut-brown eyes. She was a exceptionally blithe, dainty little maiden—a teacher of hers had remarked that she was Carrow by name and blithe by nature. Her mother derived much satisfaction from her completely faultless complexion.
{: #nw-v05-c03-p0015 }

“It brings me such joy to have a single daughter capable of wearing pink,” Mrs. Carrow was accustomed to exclaiming with delight.
{: #nw-v05-c03-p0016 }

A strong resemblance to her mother was evident in Isolde Carrow, called Izzy, who possessed hair of a red hue and eyes of gray-green that invariably gleamed with a distinct shine and radiance when twilight fell. This reason, perhaps, explained why her father favoured her most. Close companions were found in her and Edmund; he would recite his self-authored poetry solely to Izzy, making her the single individual aware that he was quietly laboring on an epic poem, one that bore a marked similarity to “Marmion” in particular aspects, though not in all. From Bess included, she guarded every one of his confidences, while sharing all of her own with him.
{: #nw-v05-c03-p0017 }

“Will those fish not be cooked shortly, Kit?” asked Bess, inhaling the aroma with her delicate nose. “I am made extremely hungry by the scent.”
{: #nw-v05-c03-p0018 }

“They are almost prepared,” stated Kit, as he deftly flipped one over. “Fetch the plates and the bread, girls. Wake up, Edmund.”
{: #nw-v05-c03-p0019 }

“What a glow the air has this evening,” Edmund remarked in a daydreaming way. It was not that fried trout was something he looked down on at all; nevertheless, nourishment for the spirit was invariably the top priority for Edmund. “The angel of flowers has traveled across the earth today, summoning the blossoms. Those blue wings of his are visible to me on that hill near the forest.”
{: #nw-v05-c03-p0020 }

“Every angel wing that ever met my sight was white,” Bess remarked.
{: #nw-v05-c03-p0021 }

“The angels of the flowers are not. A pale, misty blue describes them, exactly like the valley's haze. Oh, my desire to fly is so strong. Glorious it must be.”
{: #nw-v05-c03-p0022 }

“Occasionally, a person flies when dreaming,” Izzy remarked.
{: #nw-v05-c03-p0023 }

“It isn't precisely flying that I dream about,” Edmund remarked. “Instead, my frequent dream is that I simply lift off the earth and hover above the hedges and the trees. The feeling is wonderful—and my thought is invariably, ‘Unlike every previous time, this is no dream. It's actually happening’—and then I awaken anyway, which is devastating.”
{: #nw-v05-c03-p0024 }

“Make haste, Bess,” Kit instructed.
{: #nw-v05-c03-p0025 }

Bess had brought out the banquet-board—which was a literal board in addition to being a figurative one—from which a great deal of feasts, seasoned in a manner no food was anywhere else, had been consumed in Fern Hollow. By supporting it upon a pair of big, moss-covered stones, it was transformed into a table. The tablecloth was provided by newspapers, and the dishes were supplied by handleless cups and cracked plates taken from the items Tabitha had discarded. Bess produced salt and bread from a tin box hidden within the root of a spruce tree. Adam’s ale of unequaled clarity was furnished by the brook. As for what remained, a particular sauce, made from a mixture of young appetite and fresh air, imparted a heavenly taste to all of it. Sitting within Fern Hollow, soaked in a half-amethyst, half-gold twilight, filled with the scents of woodsy plants growing in their spring vigor and balsam-fir, surrounded everywhere by the pale stars of wild strawberry blossoms, and listening to the tinkling of bells and the soughing of the wind in the rustling tree tops while eating dry bread and fried trout, constituted an experience that the powerful individuals of the world could have envied them for.
{: #nw-v05-c03-p0026 }

“Sit in,” requested Bess, when Kit set his hissing metal plate of fish upon the table. “Kit, you are the one to offer grace.”
{: #nw-v05-c03-p0027 }

“Frying the trout was my job,” complained Kit, who disliked giving thanks before meals. “Let Edmund recite it, since he enjoys reciting grace. Also, make it brief, Walt, because I am famished.”
{: #nw-v05-c03-p0028 }

Yet no blessing, whether brief or extended, was uttered by Edmund at that moment. An event broke in upon them.
{: #nw-v05-c03-p0029 }

“Who is descending from the manse hill?” asked Izzy.
{: #nw-v05-c03-p0030 }
